stories.title: Meetings resume as Garvaghy Rd residents postpone appeal
stories.summary: The Garvaghy Road residents have temporarily postponed their court case challenging the Drumcree parade. It was due to have been heard in Belfast's Court of Appeal tomorrow. It is believed the decision was taken to allow space for mediation, which is continuing this evening. The residents had lodged a further appeal against the Parades Commission determination that said 35 Orangemen could walk along the Garvaghy Road on Sunday. A large nationalist counter demonstration meant the parade could not go ahead. The chief constable Jon Boutcher today warned the protesters they faced "criminal consequences" for blocking the parade which had been given the go-ahead by the commission. Shortly after 8pm this evening, a delegation from the Orange Order arrived at Hillsborough Castle for a meeting with British Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant.

stories.title: Residents discuss proposal, DUP MP says deal unacceptable
stories.summary: A proposed deal to resolve the Drumcree parading dispute is "not acceptable", a DUP MP has said. Carla Lockhart's assessment came after a representative of the Garvaghy Road residents said they would accept a document setting out a resolution if the Orange Order also did so. Breandán Mac Cionnaith was speaking following a meeting with British Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle. Mr Bryant has been trying to strike a compromise deal between the two sides of the standoff. Mr Mac Cionnaith said: "Obviously I can’t divulge what is in it but if it’s accepted by the Orange Order, it will be accepted by us." Portadown Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson declined to comment on the paper as he left the castle this evening.

stories.title: Labour's budget plans focus on reducing household bills
stories.summary: Labour leader Ivana Bacik has said her party is "relentlessly focused on keeping household bills down in the cost of living crisis". Publishing its alternative budget, the party is proposing targeted energy credits worth €400 to households earning less than €80,000. Further measures to tackle the soaring cost of energy include the extension of excise reductions and the reduction of VAT on home heating oil to 9%. Labour says Ireland can afford to increase core social welfare payments by €15 per week - it also wants to increase public sector pay and index income tax rates and bands in line with a projected wage growth of 4%. Labour, along with other opposition parties, is suggesting a second, targeted rate of child benefit to, as it says, "lift tens of thousands of children out of poverty". Finance spokesperson, Ged Nash, said that "the very best way to make our country fit for the future means we must declare war on child poverty, and we must mean it".

stories.title: September new electric car registrations soar 80% - SIMI
stories.summary: New figures from the Society of the Irish Motor Industry show an 80% jump in the number of new electric cars registered in September compared to the same time last year. The new SIMI figures show that 3,126 new electric cars (battery electric cars) were registered last month, compared to the 1,734 registrations in September of last year. So far this year, 35,195 new electric cars have been registered, marking a 57.3% increase compared to the same time in 2025, when 22,376 electric cars were registered. Today's figures show that overall new car registrations for September were up 13.1% to 6,342 compared to 5,607 the same time last year. Registrations so far this year are up 5.4% to 128,288 from 121,675 on the same time in 2025. Meanwhile, imported used cars saw an 18.9% increase in September to 8,326, compared to 7,000 the same month last year. Year to date imports are up 34.4% to 72,140 from 53,661 in 2025. In the new car market share by engine type, battery electric cars lead the market with a share of 27.43%, followed by hybrid (petrol electric) at 23.68%, petrol at 19.59%, plug-in hybrid at 14.93%, and diesel at 12.36%.

stories.title: Bins set alight and trams halted as French pupils protest
stories.summary: A high-school entrance hall caught fire in one French city and teenage protesters blocked trams in another as secondary pupils upped their strike over what they denounce as poor learning conditions. The movement in the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France, has seen hundreds detained in recent days. Since last week, pupils have staged protests outside schools over grievances ranging from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year's heatwaves. The protests have spread across the country from the Paris suburbs, with the government accusing hard-left politicians of encouraging the unrest. Riot police were deployed to confront the students, with the force launching internal probes after accusations of brutality against three pupils, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez. Around 340 demonstrations were under way in front of high schools by the mid-morning, with more than 160 establishments shut down as a result, police said.

stories.title: Ratings: Ireland's red-hot goalscorer stars once more
stories.summary: Double goalscorer Troy Parrott unsurprisingly rated the star man as the Republic of Ireland drew 2-2 with Austria in your archetypal game of two halves at Aviva Stadium. Gavin Bazunu was the Ireland goalkeeper generating most of the headlines over recent days, but Kelleher was always going to be first-choice here and he ensured Ireland went in ahead at half-time, pulling off a brilliant fingertip save to deny Patrick Wimmer just before Ireland scored their penalty. He also punched a dangerous cross clear when it looked like he and Dara O'Shea were about to collide and later showed good hands to keep out a Nicolas Seiwald drive from distance. Would need a post-match interview to ask what happened with second goal. Having seen Austria pull level with their two quick-fire goals, the stand-in captain decided to take matters into his own hands late on and nearly won it with a thumping strike that Florian Wiegele batted away acrobatically. O’Shea had a solid game on the right side of the back three and looked particularly assured when cutting out a dangerous Sasa Kalajdzic cross with Romano Schmid lurking with intent in the box. stories.title: McStay hopeful of 'five or six' new rules for 2027 league
stories.summary: Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group (EAG) chairman Kevin McStay is hopeful that "five or six" new rules will be officially adopted in time for the 2027 Allianz Football League - but he said that the changes will have to meet "a high threshold" to form part of the official guidelines. EAG members McStay, Séamus Kenny and Johnny Bradley addressed the media at Croke Park on Wednesday and provided more information on the 11 changes to be trialled in the upcoming Ryan Cup Division 1 campaign. A twelfth change – a return to six substitutes – will not be experimented with as the higher education competition adopts an unlimited substitute policy. Major rule adjustments that will be trialled will include a four-point goal, a ban on fisted points unless the ball is in flight, a limit on consecutive handpasses to three, a backcourt rule while breach infractions will now be able to be taken outside the 40-metre arc for a two-point attempt. The EAG will assess the data and feedback after the Ryan Cup and former Mayo and Roscommon manager McStay is hopeful that a number of proposals are greenlit in time for next season's league campaign. "We'd like to see whatever stands up going straight into the league, and then they would be formalised at Congress. I think that's possible." McStay said that any change brought for ratification will only be approved on the back on rigorous examination from multiple stakeholders, a data perspective and, also, the eye-test.

stories.title: Klopp reluctant to weigh in on Manchester City fallout
stories.summary: Former Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp said his respect for Pep Guardiola and the Manchester City sides that battled Liverpool in some of the Premier League's closest title races has left him reluctant to comment on the fallout from City's financial rules case. City were found guilty of serious financial breaches by an independent commission on Tuesday, though the club have denied wrongdoing and are expected to appeal, with sanctions yet to be determined. The 59-year-old, whose Liverpool side twice finished a point behind City, had previously joked that he would attend a parade if Liverpool were retrospectively awarded titles but said he no longer felt that way. "I haven't given it much thought, even though I've seen it of course," Klopp told reporters on Wednesday. "I also know what I said about it in the past and how if there's ever a parade I'll be there, but it doesn't feel like that anymore. "My respect for Pep Guardiola and the football played at City during the time we played against each other... plus what an opponent they proved to be for us at the very highest level is far too great for me to be able to say anything now."

stories.title: Second row O'Tighearnaigh on juggling medicine and rugby
stories.summary: Conor O'Tighearnaigh could be said to represent something of a throwback. Back in the days when playing rugby was officially a hobby for even those at the highest level, there were plenty of doctors and would-be doctors in the international game. stories.title: Everyone is a writer now — but what does being a writer mean?
stories.summary: I've taught creative writing for years, in universities, writers’ centres, libraries and festivals, online and in person, and the people who come to these courses are always wildly different. Some have been writing for decades, others have barely written anything since school and arrive nervous, apologising before they have even read a sentence aloud. Some are hugely talented and some are not, which is a difficult and sometimes unpopular thing to say, but it makes it no less true. More and more, the conversation turns towards publication. How do I get an agent? How do I know when the novel is ready? Why am I still being rejected? People tell me they have done five courses, ten courses, an MA, sometimes another MA, and are confused that nothing has happened. They have spent the money, taken the feedback and rewritten the novel. Surely they should be published by now. I understand the ambition. I did an undergraduate degree in English, then a Masters in Creative Writing, then a PhD in Creative Writing, which is a ridiculous amount of time to spend studying something that guarantees no job or success at the end of it. I wrote a novel that went out to publishers and received beautiful rejections, editors writing long emails about what they admired before explaining that they would not be publishing it. Not everyone who writes will be published, and not everyone who writes should be. That does not mean they should stop. That novel remains unpublished. During the years I spent writing it, I was working, teaching, living abroad, getting married and having children. I was building a life that did not look as though it would include being a novelist. Still, I wasn’t waiting for my real life to begin. I loved books, was thirsty for knowledge and wanted to write better. The novel going nowhere doesn’t take that away.

stories.summary: Returning for its fourth series, the new run will also see the return of The Parish Quiz, which this week features Jack English from Adare, Co. Limerick playing against Laura Collins of Scartaglen, Co. Kerry. Zamparelli will talk about her television career, revisit her hidden-camera antics on The Fear, and share stories about married life with her husband, Lau. Regan will explain the difference between "a gob****e and an eejit", share his experiences of being an Irishman abroad, and reveal why the Irish accent is a superpower overseas. Paddy McDonnell joins the show from Belfast to perform a stand-up set, and Galway trad act Clada will play Step It Out Mary. Speaking about the new season, Johnny Smacks says, "We're absolutely delighted to be back for Season 4 of The Late Night Lock In. When we started the show, the idea was basically to bring the craic of a great Irish night out onto the telly - a bit of music, brilliant guests, plenty of messing and absolutely no guarantee that Johnny B will stick to the running order. Johnny B adds, "The best thing about The Late Night Lock In is that it doesn’t feel like a normal TV show. It feels like you’ve landed into a pub on a Thursday night, found yourself sitting beside someone you never expected to meet, the band starts playing and suddenly you’re staying for one more.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (October 2-4)
stories.summary: From Halloween headpieces to Baroque A Cappella, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. BuzzFest - Phibsboro's Community, Sustainability & Biodiversity Festival - returns for its 10th year on Saturday, 3 October. The festival will run from 12.30pm to 4pm in the Scouts Hall (located behind the library) with an amazing selection of stalls, stands, talks, workshops, repair cafe, music, food and craic. This includes a Halloween headpiece workshop inspired by collage art and fuelled by love for scavenging. All materials provided. The workshop will last 40 minutes and is aimed at those 6+. Tickets €2 on Eventbrite. Eatyard brings a slice of Bavaria to Drumcondra this October, with a series of beers*, pretzels, music, bands, fun & games running from Sept 24th - Oct 24th at The Bernard Shaw. Expect a whole host of German games to dig your teeth into, including Stein-Holding competitions, Hasselhoff karaoke, Lederhösen Limbo, the spicy currywurst challenge, live music & much more. Tickets €16.97 on Eventbrite. The event is for those 20+. Dublin Mountains Festival (Féile na Sléibhte) runs from 1-10 October, celebrating nature through community-driven events. On Friday, 2 October, a walk and talk with tree planting at Barnaslingan Wood will take place, led by the Coillte team overseeing the Dublin Mountains Makeover project. Reserve a spot on Eventbrite. Mother x Absolut present Daytime Dance Party: The Doll Edition On Saturday, 3 October, The George will play host to a very special edition of the Daytime Dance Party series. Trans, intersex and non-binary people will be celebrated with a jam-packed lineup including Glamo, Shrem, Mars Montana, Ruth Kavanagh, Shaqira Knightly, Toni & Tony, Dr Count Evil, Anziety, and Queeen Marie. Tickets are €5.58, with ticket revenue going to the Transgender Equality Network Ireland.

A Family Liaison Officer (FLO) continues to provide support to the family of the deceased.

stories.title: 5% of Ireland job postings mention data centres - Indeed
stories.summary: Just under 5% of all job postings on the Indeed hiring platform now mention data centres. This is roughly double the percentage share seen between 2019 and 2025 and, according to Indeed, the highest proportion among ten European countries analysed by the platform. Indeed's research also found that European employers advertise higher pay for data centre roles than for the same occupations elsewhere. "The largest premiums are generally seen among workers directly tied to data centre sites, including installation and maintenance roles," according to Indeed. Pawel Adrjan, Senior Director of Economic Research for EMEA and APAC at Indeed, said data centre hiring is one of the few areas of growth in tech-adjacent hiring at a time when wider tech postings remain under pressure. "Ireland stands out particularly strongly, with nearly 5% of job postings now mentioning a data centre, roughly twice the share we have seen in recent years," Mr Adrjan said.

stories.title: Legal advice sought over Garda protected disclosure
stories.summary: The Minister for Justice has sought legal advice following allegations made about the handling of a protected disclosure concerning Garda equipment, Tánaiste Simon Harris has told the Dáil. He was responding during Leaders' Questions to Aontú TD Paul Lawless who said that a whistleblower made a protected disclosure in September 2023 claiming that gun holsters used by members of An Garda Síochána were faulty and dangerous. Mr Lawless said the disclosure alleged warnings about the holsters had been ignored and that the matter directly implicated Garda Commissioner Drew Harris. The Aontú TD accused the then Minister for Justice Helen MeEntee, of breaking the law in her handling of the matter. Mr Lawless also asked Mr Harris what role he had played, while serving as Minister for Justice, in a decision to refer a separate protected disclosure concerning faulty ammunition back to An Garda Síochána. Simon Harris said that the Oireachtas must uphold the laws governing protected disclosures and noted that the Protected Disclosures Act was designed to remove politicians from the investigation of workplace wrongdoing complaints in State agencies.

stories.title: Manufacturing output hits more than four year high - PMI
stories.summary: The manufacturing sector accelerated in September as production grew at its fastest pace since March 2022 and demand remained firm in domestic and overseas markets, a business survey showed today. The latest AIB Ireland Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, rose to 55.5 in September from 55.4 in August, a survey by S&P Global showed. "Output rose rapidly in September, increasing to the highest level since March 2022, with respondents citing continued robust order books," said David McNamara, AIB's chief economist. Production growth was the sharpest since March 2022, and new orders rose for a 21st month in a row. Total new work expanded at a slightly softer rate than August's 52-month high. Export orders increased, with the seasonally adjusted New Export Orders Index reaching its highest level since June. Firms cited stronger business inflows from major developed markets. Employment growth was unchanged from August's seven-month low.

stories.title: US government's new AI chatbot stops debunking Trump
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump unveiled what he called a "damn good" AI chatbot, but it quickly drew attention for contradicting some of his contentious political claims. A day later, however, it stopped answering some political questions. "Hello, America. Whatever you need from government, start here," reads the America.gov platform, which Mr Trump launched in a bid to simplify access to government information and federal services. The chatbot soon began contradicting Mr Trump on controversial subjects such as the 2020 presidential election, which he wrongly claims to have won, and the 6 January 2021 insurrection that saw a violent mob attacking the US Capitol. "On its first day, America.gov harnessed facts and official documents to contradict some of the false narratives and political framing about immigration and elections heavily promoted by the administration that built it," said the Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas. "Initial analyses found that America.gov generally provided evidence-based answers backed by government records, even when those records contradicted claims made by Trump and his administration."

stories.title: Hallgrimsson sees positives as 'tiredness' halts Ireland
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson has pointed to fatigue as the reason his squad squandered a two-goal lead to draw 2-2 with Austria on Thursday. A Troy Parrott wonder goal gave Ireland the lead early into the game, before the Real Betis striker added a second from the penalty spot before the break. However, goals from Alexander Prass and Michael Gregoritsch within six minutes of one another ended Irish hopes of topping the group at the halfway stage of the UEFA Nations League B group phase. "We knew, and I told you before the game, this team is high energy; and we knew that we needed to do some rotation and changes. I felt like we just lost organisation, probably due to tiredness, and then you start to make mistakes. "That was something that we were obviously not happy with, but the first half was good, the organisation was good, we know we can do this. "I kind of expected us to get out of gas at some point, but maybe not so quickly. This week has been not only physically difficult, (but) it's been mentally difficult and that takes a lot of energy as well."

stories.title: Fitzmaurice leading candidate to succeed Joyce in Galway
stories.summary: Éamonn Fitzmaurice is in advanced talks with the Galway County Board to take over the manager's position vacated by Pádraic Joyce in early September. It is understood the Finuge clubman has engaged positively with Galway chairman Paul Bellew in recent weeks and is the leading candidate to take charge of the Tribesmen's senior footballers. A three-time All-Ireland winner as a player, Fitzmaurice managed Kerry for six years between 2013 and 2018, leading the Kingdom to Sam Maguire glory in 2014. He also claimed six straight Munster SFC titles and an Allianz League title during his time in charge. He remained involved with the club scene in his native Kerry, coaching the Clifford brothers' club Fossa in 2022 as they claimed a junior All-Ireland title. He was one of the most prominent members of the Football Review Committee, which introduced, trialled and refined the new playing rules that many see as having a revitalising effect on the game since their introduction in 2015.

stories.title: De Zerbi receives backing of Tottenham's chief executive
stories.summary: Chief executive Vinai Venkatesham has offered his backing to Roberto De Zerbi after Tottenham's poor start to the new campaign. Spurs are bottom of the Premier League and winless after five fixtures despite a summer of lavish spending where more than £380million (€444m) was committed on new players. However, Venkatesham pointed to the "underlying performances" with Tottenham able to create plenty of good openings without scoring in matches against Newcastle, Nottingham Forest and Everton. Speaking during last week’s first Fan Advisory Board meeting of the season, Venkatesham noted he was "encouraged by aspects of the underlying performances since the opening day defeat (at Brentford)." The Spurs CEO "acknowledged the disappointment at the current points total even at this early point in the season and recognised the frustration this caused supporters following the previous campaign". Venkatesham was quick to point out his belief in De Zerbi and the revamped playing group after 10 new signings joined along with the departures of experienced players like Guglielmo Vicario, Djed Spence, Cristian Romero, Kevin Danso and Joao Palhinha.

stories.title: Crowley targeting Christmas return amid injury layoff
stories.summary: Jack Crowley is still hoping to return to Munster action at some point over the festive period, but has acknowledged ongoing uncertainty on how his body will recover from a vascular lower limb injury that has kept him out since April. After missing the end of Munster's domestic campaign and Ireland’s Nations Championship tests in July, with the restart of the URC, Champions Cup and November internationals also coming too soon, the out-half says that a lengthy period on the sidelines has once again "highlighted my love for the game". As the start of this new season approached, Munster head coach Clayton McMillan confirmed that Crowley had suffered a "narrowing of a (blood) vessel". Crowley explained that the issue left him unable to run or kick a rugby ball, but that he was not hindered away from the pitch. "Please God that when it comes to Christmas, I’ll be fully fit," he said. "I’m currently in a period of just rest. It’s just allowing everything to heal, to get strong. From that period return to exercise. I can do upper body work but in terms of running and stuff, that’s not happening right now."

stories.title: Druid explores O'Neill's A Moon for the Misbegotten
stories.summary: Patrick Lonergan explores the history of Eugene O'Neill's theatrical masterpiece A Moon for the Misbegotten, revived by Druid Theatre Company and coming to Gaiety Theatre this October for the Dublin Theatre Festival. A Moon for the Misbegotten was the last play that Eugene O'Neill ever completed, and its elegiac tone makes it feel like it might have been his own unconscious farewell to playwriting. He described his play as a "fine, unusual, tragic comedy" – and its blend of humour and sadness is indeed both fine and unusual. The play is deeply autobiographical, drawing on the figure of O’Neill’s brother Jamie, an actor who had drunk himself to death when he was only 45. Reimagining his brother as James Tyrone, O’Neill confines that character to a single place and a single 24-hour-period, so that he can grapple with the possibility of finding love with Josie, a young Irish-American woman. What follows is a battle between both characters’ competing desires: for love, reputation, ownership of land – and for just one more drink. Irishness is central to those conflicts. The play’s stage directions say of Josie that the "map of Ireland is stamped on her face" – an old Irish-American saying that was intended to suggest distinctively Irish features. But in one of many connections between the two characters, the same phrasing is used to describe Tyrone too – not in Moon but in A Long Day’s Journey Into Night, a companion play that O’Neill wrote between 1939 and 1941, but which was not staged until after his death. That link reveals O’Neill’s desire to present Tyrone and Josie both as psychologically complex individuals and as emblematically Irish. Writing about them thus became a way for him to map Ireland, and to think about its multifaceted influence on American life. That theme is apparent from the first act, when Josie and her father – a tenant farmer called Phil Hogan – are trying to frighten off a neighbouring landowner. They do so by playing on the stereotypes associated with their nationality: they are buoyant and comical – but also menacing, as if their buffoonery could tip into violence at any moment. They are, in other words, like characters in a stage Irish play.

stories.title: Maura Higgins continues to impress on DWTS US
stories.summary: Longford native Maura Higgins continued her good run on Dancing with the Stars US on Wednesday, finishing second on the leaderboard at the end of the night. The 35-year-old former Love Island contestant performed a Quickstep with her professional partner Mark Ballas to George Benson's Turn Your Love Around. There was a tie for first place between Amber Glenn and Harry Shum Jr, who both received a score of 24, while Higgins and Ballas followed closely behind with 22 points out of 30. Commenting after her dance, judge Derek Hough described Higgins’ topline as "exquisite" and said the performance was a "masterclass in elegance". Fellow judge Bruno Tonioli also compared Higgins to Audrey Hepburn, praising the "lightness and crispness" of her footwork. Judge Carrie Ann Inaba highlighted Higgins' remarkable posture, telling the other contestants: "THAT is what you’re going for!"

stories.title: 4 spots in Ireland among winners at the World Spa Awards 2026
stories.summary: Four destinations on the island of Ireland have been named as winners in the World Spa Awards 2026. The annual awards ceremony is now in its 12th year and "serves to celebrate and reward excellence in spa and wellness tourism", according to its website. Founded in 2015 to highlight the successes of the wellness industry, the awards connect spa specialists and celebrate the leaders in the industry, which has boomed in popularity in recent years. Spas and hotels enter the awards themselves, and once a shortlist has been created industry experts are invited to vote online for their top picks. Ireland received four awards across two categories: day spas and hotel spas. Eden Elements at the luxurious Eden One spa in Ballsbridge, Dublin was named Dublin's best day spa, its fifth consecutive year securing the award.

stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel will get to the "root" of the co-pilot who engaged ⁠in a foiled attempt to crash an Israel-bound flydubai flight and that Israel will "possibly" be participating in the probe into the incident. Disaster was averted on yesterday's flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, which was carrying 170 passengers, after the wounded captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers to subdue the attacker and a reserve crew that had been on board to land the plane in Saudi Arabia. The flight plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds as it flew over Saudi Arabia before the ‌passengers and crew managed to subdue the attacker and land the plane. Mr Netanyahu said the attacker was being investigated in Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed at Tabuk airport, and that he believed he would be taken to the United Arab Emirates. "We'll be following and possibly also participating in this investigation," Mr Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity. Asked if there was any indication of Iranian involvement, Mr Netanyahu said it was too early to say.

stories.title: Cost of policing Drumcree stand-off at £3m so far - PSNI
stories.summary: The cost of policing the Drumcree stand-off has so far cost £3 million, PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has said. Mr Boutcher has been speaking publicly for the first time in the five-day stand-off, addressing a public session of the Northern Ireland Policing Board this morning. He said the police objective was to facilitate the Parades Commission determination that had approved the parade of 35 Orangemen along the Garvaghy Road. "Without that determination such a parade would be unlawful. What it does not mean is that the police must accommodate that determination at all costs," he said. Mr Boutcher said he also had a statutory responsibility to preserve the peace and maintain order. "We are not back in 1997. We are not expected to, nor will we, force members of the Orange Order, many of whom are of a certain age, through a hostile crowd which will be unsafe and will be disproportionate and where the wider consequences for Northern Ireland could be catastrophic."

stories.title: Irish players 'exposed, hung out to dry' by FAI - Ennis
stories.summary: Social Democrats TD and Spokesperson on Sport Daniel Ennis has said the Ireland players "have been hung out to dry" by the FAI and the board of the association should resign. The FAI is to tell the Oireachtas Sports Committee today how the decision to proceed with the controversial fixtures against Israel was made in the best interests of Irish football. The CEO of the FAI David Courell and other senior figures at the Association will answer questions from TDs and Senators this afternoon with Ireland to play Israel again on Sunday in the UEFA Nations League after preparations for last weekend's fixture in Hungary were thrown into chaos at the eleventh hour. He said it is the biggest crisis facing Irish football, with many people telling him that they will not renew season tickets. Mr Ennis said that the FAI has put "a dark stain" on Irish football. In relation to possible sanctions that the FAI may have faced for not playing the match, Mr Ennis said that "no sanction stands up against the charred remains of babies."

stories.title: Profits at RTÉ commercial arm hit by sale of GAAGo
stories.summary: Operating profits last year remained flat at €11.3m but the €487,000 share of profit that the company booked from its GAA GO joint venture in 2024 was no longer available resulting in the drop in pre-tax profits. The note states that "the locked box date with regard to the sale of the company's share in GAAGo was December 31st 2024, hence no share in profit in 2025". The directors state that Digital Player Licensing was the primary source of income for the firm in 2025 at €7.9m "although this was slightly behind 2024, due to the non-renewal of one licensing arrangement". Revenues generated by Programme Interaction Competitions (PIC) stabilised last year and remained consistent with 2024 after being impacted over the past few years by declining levels of audience engagement with TV competitions. Sales of Love/Hate, Smother and The Clinic to TV stations overseas helped programme sales increase by over 90% in 2024 and the directors state that for 2025 "TV Programmes sales were significantly down on prior year". "However, as noted at the time, 2024 was an unprecedented year for programme sales, in particular across drama," they state.

stories.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'catastrophic' melt in 2026
stories.summary: Switzerland's glaciers, which are disproportionately impacted by climate change, have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts have said, with 2026 registering the second-biggest melt on record. Swiss glaciers saw 5.5% of their volume melt away this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study, published after a record hot summer preceded by a winter with little snowfall. "The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice," said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss, describing 2026 as "a catastrophic year". Perched on the Scex Rouge glacier, at an altitude of nearly 3,000 metres, he gazed across the landscape in despair. He carefully dismantled the four-metre-long aluminium measurement stake inserted at the centre of the glacier. In late July, when it was installed, it was completely embedded, but now more than three metres protrude from the grey surface of the ice.

stories.title: Garcia files to have LIV Golf contract terminated
stories.summary: Sergio Garcia is pursuing the termination of his LIV Golf contract, a potential path out of the league. As LIV Golf works toward fulfilling a restructuring agreement following Chapter 11 ⁠bankruptcy protection, Garcia's attorney argued in a six-page courtfiling on Wednesday that termination "should not be objectionable" to the league because it "is consistent with (LIV Golf's) statement that the agreement is 'not part of (LIV Golf's) go-forward business plan.'" The Spaniard's camp further argued that with the contract still in place, "tournament organisers, sponsors and other counterparties may hesitate before dealing with Garcia, who may be unable to represent that they are free of competing contractual commitments". LIV ‌Golf is attempting to ⁠continue in 2027 and beyond under a so-called "LIV2.0" business plan after the Saudi Public Investment Fund withdrew its support. The league has a restructuring agreement with BC Partners Credit, but it includes conditions that must be fulfilled within 35 days of LIV's bankruptcy filing. At least 50 % of players with financial claims against the league must agree to participate in LIV 2.0, and that group must ⁠also represent at least two-thirds of the total dollar amount of player ‌claims. Golf Channel reported that LIV Golf has secured more than enough ⁠verbal commitments to ‌exceed the conditional threshold. The league's deadline is 13 October.
